summary:
Vatican City presents essentially no criminal-law exposure to a trans visitor. No documented criminal-law persecution of consensual homosexual conduct has occurred in Vatican City in modern times, and decriminalisation has nineteenth-century roots. Nothing about being trans is criminalised, and there are no bathroom inspections, no morality police, and no policing of tourist gender expression by the gendarmerie or the Swiss Guards.

Vatican City operates no prison system. Only a few cells are maintained for pre-trial detention, and anyone sentenced to imprisonment serves the term in an Italian prison with the costs borne by Vatican City. Because no domestic prison system exists, there is no trans-specific prisoner-placement policy, no trans custody facility, and no documented case of a trans prisoner being placed anywhere in this jurisdiction.

Entry is made through the neighbouring city of Rome across an open border, with no border formality and no gender-related screening. Millions of visitors of every presentation pass through each year without incident.

No legal recognition of gender exists in Vatican City. No anti-discrimination protection, no facilities rule, and no document-amendment mechanism covers a visitor or a resident.

The Holy See's institutional posture toward homosexuality and gender is openly hostile, and this drives policy even though it does not translate into criminal law against visitors. In October 2008 Catholic officials refused to accept France's first-choice candidate as ambassador to the Holy See because he is gay, forcing Paris to appoint a different envoy; this is a documented instance of the Vatican government rejecting an LGBT person in diplomatic relations. In 2019 the Vatican's Congregation for Catholic Education published 'Male and Female He Created Them', which opposes what it calls gender theory, stating that it 'denies the difference and reciprocity in nature of a man and a woman' and 'eliminates the anthropological basis of the family'.

The current Holy See posture on same-sex couples is set by the DDF declaration Fiducia Supplicans, issued on 20 March 2023 under Pope Francis, which permits spontaneous blessings for same-sex couples while forbidding any rite resembling marriage; a January 2024 DDF press release reiterated that blessings never extend to the unions themselves. No partner recognition or marriage equivalence follows from this for a visitor or a resident.
tangentialFactors:
The legal baseline of Vatican City is best read as distinct from the Church's diplomacy and teaching. The 2019 education document and the 2008 ambassadorial rejection are acts of the Holy See as an institution and as a diplomatic actor; neither creates an offence enforceable against a person inside the city-state. A visitor therefore faces the ordinary tourist-policing environment of a very small enclave rather than a morality regime, while still encountering an official culture that treats homosexuality and gender non-conformity as errors to be corrected.

Detention exposure runs through a neighbouring jurisdiction rather than through Vatican facilities. The few cells available are for pre-trial holding only, so any custodial outcome would place a person, at Vatican expense, in an Italian prison under that country's prisoner-classification rules, including its rules on the placement of transgender detainees. That transfer mechanism, not any Vatican policy, is where a trans-specific custody risk would arise.
localsOnly:
Residents of Vatican City have no route to legal gender recognition, no mechanism to amend a gender marker on a document, and no statutory anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity or sexual orientation. Employment discipline and institutional standing for the small resident population, overwhelmingly employees of the Holy See, rest on church law and internal regulation rather than on any civil anti-discrimination statute.

Anyone convicted of an offence by Vatican authority serves the sentence in an Italian prison, funded by Vatican City. The territory maintains no prison of its own and therefore has no prison rules, no cell-assignment policy, and no visiting regime of its own to which a trans detainee could be subject.
outOfScopeNotes:
No United States State Department Holy See chapter for 2023 or 2024 was available for this entry, and several claims rest on encyclopedic sources used as a last resort rather than on primary legal texts or government reporting. The criminal-law baseline and the absence of a prison system are stated on that basis.

Unresolved: whether the Congregation for Catholic Education's 2019 document or the 2023 declaration Fiducia Supplicans carries any operative civil-law effect inside Vatican City, as opposed to guiding church institutions worldwide, is not sourced here. Rules on gender markers in travel or identity documents issued to Vatican residents, and any procedure for changing them, are likewise not sourced; no document-amendment mechanism was located. The precise legal basis of the open border arrangement with Italy is described here only as it affects entry screening.
